# Preliminaries {.unnumbered}

## About These Notes

These notes support STAT 3255/5255, Introduction to Data Science, at the
University of Connecticut. They introduce the ideas, tools, and working habits
needed to learn from data in a reproducible and responsible way.

The notes are written as a Quarto book and use Python for computation. They are
intended to remain useful across semesters and to develop over time into a
textbook. The instructor-authored book is the authoritative source for the
course content. Semester schedules, assignments, and student-contributed notes
are maintained separately.

## Building the Book

To build the notes locally:

1. Clone the source repository.
2. Create and activate a Python virtual environment in the repository root.
3. Install the dependencies specified by the project environment files.
4. Supply any credentials required by particular examples through the
   documented local configuration. Never commit credentials to Git.
5. Run `quarto render` from the repository root.

Quarto writes the rendered book to `_book/`. Generated output and local caches
are not tracked by Git; the source and environment specifications are.

## Learning Data Science in the Age of AI

The concern that artificial intelligence will replace entry-level analytical
work is reasonable. AI systems can already write routine code, clean data,
create visualizations, fit models, and draft reports. Consequently, a course
that consists mainly of memorizing commands or reproducing standard analyses
would offer diminishing value. The appropriate response, however, is not to
abandon data-science education. It is to teach the knowledge and judgment
needed to use increasingly capable tools well.

Current evidence presents both disruption and opportunity. In its 2025 survey,
the World Economic Forum reported that 41 percent of employers expected to
reduce their workforce where AI could automate tasks, while 77 percent planned
to upskill their workers. The same report identified AI and big data as the
fastest-growing skill area and analytical thinking as the most widely valued
core skill [@worldeconomicforum2025]. In the United States, the Bureau of Labor
Statistics projects employment of data scientists to grow by about 34 percent
from 2024 to 2034 [@bls2025datascientists]. Such projections are not a promise
of a job, but they do show why students need a combination of technical
knowledge and analytical judgment rather than less preparation.

AI tends to amplify the capabilities of its user rather than make expertise
irrelevant. A person with limited understanding may use AI to produce a weak
analysis faster, more confidently, and in more polished language. A strong
researcher can use the same technology to investigate more alternatives,
challenge assumptions, detect errors, and undertake work that would previously
have required much more time. The difference is not merely skill in writing
prompts. It is the ability to conceive, direct, and evaluate an analysis.

First, students need enough knowledge to recognize **what is possible**. A
useful analysis begins before any code is written: someone must connect a
substantive problem to data that could inform it, distinguish descriptive,
predictive, causal, and decision questions, and recognize promising methods.
Without this foundation, a user can ask AI only for familiar tasks and may not
notice when a question cannot be answered from the available data. Knowledge
expands both the range and the ambition of what a student can imagine doing.

Second, students must learn **how to direct AI**. A vague real-world concern
must be translated into precise questions, variables, comparisons, and
computational steps. The user must supply context, state constraints, decide
what evidence would be relevant, and revise the approach as new problems
emerge. These are central data-science skills. AI can assist with their
execution, but it cannot compensate reliably for a poorly formulated problem.

Third, students must be able to **evaluate what AI produces**. Plausible code
may contain subtle errors; an attractive graph may conceal a misleading
comparison; a highly accurate model may suffer from data leakage; and a fluent
report may make a causal claim that the study design cannot support. Evaluation
therefore requires understanding data provenance, measurement, variation,
validation, uncertainty, reproducibility, and the context in which a result
will be used. Because AI can make incorrect work appear polished and
authoritative, these foundations become more important, not less.

This course prepares students to work with AI without surrendering judgment to
it. Students learn enough about data, computation, statistical reasoning, and
communication to formulate worthwhile questions, supervise computational
work, verify results, explain limitations, and take responsibility for the
conclusions they present. The goal is not to compete with AI at producing code
quickly. It is to become the kind of informed practitioner whose abilities are
made stronger by AI.

## Adapting to Rapid Skill Acquisition

Data science requires learning new tools and ideas quickly. VanderPlas
[@vanderplas2016python] captures an important feature of this work:

> When a technologically-minded person is asked to help a friend, family
> member, or colleague with a computer problem, most of the time it's less a
> matter of knowing the answer as much as knowing how to quickly find an
> unknown answer. In data science it's the same: searchable web resources such
> as online documentation, mailing-list threads, and StackOverflow answers
> contain a wealth of information, even (especially?) if it is a topic you've
> found yourself searching before. Being an effective practitioner of data
> science is less about memorizing the tool or command you should use for every
> possible situation, and more about learning to effectively find the
> information you don't know, whether through a web search engine or another
> means.

Effective practitioners learn how to frame a problem, consult documentation
and other reliable sources, test possible solutions, and evaluate whether the
result makes sense.

This habit is especially important when software, data formats, and computing
environments change. Encountering an unfamiliar package, error message, data
source, or hardware requirement is part of the work. The goal is to develop a
repeatable way to investigate such problems rather than to accumulate isolated
recipes.

## Working Principles

The examples and exercises in this book emphasize a few recurring principles:

- Start with a clear question and understand the context of the data.
- Keep raw data separate from derived data and analysis output.
- Explore data interactively, then collect tested code into reproducible
  scripts or documents.
- Consider during data cleaning how each variable will be used later.
- Use version control to make small, understandable changes.
- Document data sources, assumptions, software dependencies, and decisions.
- Check results for statistical, computational, and contextual plausibility.
- Communicate the question, evidence, limitations, and conclusion—not merely
  the code.

For presentations, introduce the problem and motivate why it matters. Give the
audience a map of the talk, emphasize the main results, and conclude with the
central takeaway. Original examples and careful attribution make an explanation
both clearer and more trustworthy.
